meta.abstract: Marvell Technology, Inc. (MRVL, NASDAQ) is the Santa Clara-headquartered fabless semiconductor company that has, in the eight years since Matt Murphy became CEO in July 2016, transformed from a networking-and-storage chip vendor into one of the two structurally-important US merchant suppliers of AI-data-centre custom silicon — alongside Broadcom. The company traces its origins to the 1995 founding by Dr. Sehat Sutardja, his wife Weili Dai, and brother Pantas Sutardja as a fabless networking-chip startup. Through the 2000s and 2010s Marvell scaled across storage controllers (the disk-drive read-channel business that anchored early revenue), Ethernet networking silicon, and broader connectivity products. The strategic re-orientation under Murphy was deliberate: the 2018 $6 billion acquisition of Cavium added the ThunderX Arm server processor and the LiquidIO networking accelerator portfolios; the 2019 acquisition of Avera Semiconductor (the former IBM custom-silicon ASIC group) added custom-ASIC design capability at advanced process nodes; the 2020 $10 billion acquisition of Inphi added the PAM-DSP coherent-optics IP and the hyperscaler-data-centre optical interconnect customer relationships; the 2022 $1.1 billion acquisition of Innovium added the Teralynx switch-silicon line that competes directly with Broadcom Tomahawk. The current product franchise sits across five reporting segments: Data Center (the dominant growth driver, anchored by custom-ASIC programmes for hyperscalers and the PAM-DSP / Teralynx / electro-optics portfolios), Enterprise Networking, Carrier Infrastructure, Consumer, and Automotive/Industrial. Fiscal year 2026 (ended early February 2026) produced annual revenue of approximately $7.0-7.5 billion with Data Center contributing well over half of the mix at materially higher gross margins than the legacy segments. The custom-ASIC backlog with Amazon (Trainium custom silicon), Microsoft (Maia 2 generation custom silicon), Google (TPU adjacent collaboration), and emerging hyperscaler programmes has been publicly characterised by management as multi-billion-dollar over the multi-year contracted horizon. CEO Matt Murphy continues to lead the company through this strategic transformation alongside an executive bench including President and COO Chris Koopmans, CFO Willem Meintjes (joined September 2024 from Pure Storage), and the deep technology leadership inherited from the Cavium, Inphi, and Innovium acquisitions. The investment proposition compresses AI custom-silicon design-win sustainability, the structural duopoly with Broadcom at the hyperscaler ASIC layer, the optical-interconnect cycle continuation, and the legacy-segment headwinds in Enterprise Networking and Carrier.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Structural Shift

Marvell Technology Group (MRVL, NASDAQ) entered fiscal year 2024 as a diversified semiconductor company in which its Data Center segment accounted for roughly 39 percent of revenue. By the close of fiscal year 2026 — the twelve months ending January 2026 — that segment had crossed $6.1 billion, representing approximately 74 percent of a total revenue base that had itself expanded to a record $8.195 billion. The migration was not incremental. It was a structural repricing of what Marvell is: a custom-silicon and electro-optics franchise operating at the intersection of hyperscaler capital expenditure and the AI infrastructure buildout.

Incorporated in Delaware and operationally headquartered in Santa Clara, California, Marvell reports five segments: Data Center (the principal growth franchise, encompassing custom ASIC, electro-optics, and Ethernet switch silicon), Enterprise Networking, Carrier Infrastructure, Automotive/Industrial, and Consumer. The last three have served, across the AI cycle, as a mechanical drag on headline revenue that substantially understated the rate of acceleration in the company's strategic core.

Matt Murphy has been President and Chief Executive Officer since July 2016, recruited from Maxim Integrated where he had served as a Group President. His nearly decade-long tenure is the structural through-line of the transformation. Chris Koopmans, who joined through the 2018 Cavium acquisition, serves as Chief Operating Officer with broad responsibility across the product portfolio. Willem Meintjes, who joined Marvell in 2016 and was promoted through the Chief Accounting Officer and Treasurer roles before assuming the Chief Financial Officer position in January 2023, has presided over the financial architecture of the AI inflection. Marc van Zadelhoff, formerly Chief Executive of Devo Technology and Mimecast, became Chairman in 2024.

## The Acquisition Arc

The Data Center segment's composition today is largely the product of four acquisitions executed under Murphy between 2018 and 2022. Cavium, closed in July 2018 for approximately $6 billion, brought ARM-architecture ThunderX server processors, LiquidIO networking accelerators, and the engineering culture of a merchant network-processor company. Avera Semiconductor, acquired from GlobalFoundries in September 2019 for approximately $650 million, contributed IBM-heritage custom ASIC design services and a client base in the high-reliability enterprise and communications market — the technical DNA from which Marvell's hyperscaler custom-silicon practice subsequently developed. Inphi, closed in April 2021 for approximately $10 billion, was the transformative deal: it brought PAM-DSP coherent-optics intellectual property and, critically, established customer relationships with hyperscalers for optical interconnect — the $10 billion price tag implicitly valuing both the technology and the bookings pipeline. Innovium, acquired in October 2022 for approximately $1.1 billion, added Teralynx switch silicon, placing Marvell in direct competition with Broadcom's Tomahawk line inside hyperscaler data centres.

## Revenue Architecture, FY2023–FY2026

| Fiscal year | Total revenue (USD) | Data Center share |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $5.92 billion | ~33% |
| FY2024 | $5.51 billion | ~39% |
| FY2025 | $5.77 billion | ~50% |
| FY2026 | $8.195 billion | ~74% |

The 42 percent revenue expansion in FY2026 against a prior-year base of $5.77 billion was driven almost entirely by Data Center, which grew 46 percent year-on-year to $6.1 billion. The first quarter of fiscal 2027 — reported in May 2026 — produced [total revenue of $1.895 billion](https://investor.marvell.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/95/marvell-technology-inc-reports-first-quarter-of-fiscal-year-2026-financial-results), up 63 percent year-on-year, with the Data Center segment at $1.44 billion, or 76 percent of total revenue.

## Custom Silicon: From Zero to $1.5 Billion

The custom-ASIC business — internally characterised as the XPU franchise — scaled from effectively zero revenue at the start of fiscal 2024 to approximately $1.5 billion across the full fiscal year 2026, supported by programmes with Amazon (Trainium, the training accelerator), Microsoft (Maia 200 and the subsequent Maia 300 generation), and Google (TPU-adjacent and Axion ARM CPU co-development work), as well as an emerging Meta data-processing-unit engagement and a broader portfolio of cloud-provider wins that [management characterised as 18 design wins](https://tech-insider.org/marvell-technology-stock-surge-custom-ai-chip-2026/) at the most recent update. A new, undisclosed Tier 1 XPU programme was flagged for high-volume production ramp in the forward guidance.

Murphy set out the trajectory explicitly in the Q4 FY2026 earnings call:

> "We've scaled from 0 revenue to $1.5 billion in fiscal 2026 ... custom revenue to at least double year over year" in fiscal 2028.

The programmes run through Sandeep Bharathi's Custom Compute and Storage organisation, which manages advanced-node execution at TSMC — 3-nanometre for current-generation Trainium and next-generation Maia tape-outs, with 2-nanometre capacity secured for subsequent generations. CoWoS packaging, the advanced substrate technology required for high-bandwidth-memory integration in AI accelerators, is procured through the same TSMC supply chain that serves Nvidia's H-series and B-series products.

## The Optical Interconnect Franchise

The Inphi acquisition's most durable strategic contribution is the electro-optics product line, led by Loi Nguyen as Executive Vice President. The PAM-DSP architecture that Inphi pioneered has progressed through 100G, 400G, and 800G generations, each adoption wave driven by hyperscaler data-centre interconnect density requirements. The 1.6T generation, underpinned by Marvell's 2-nanometre coherent DSP, represents the next upgrade cycle. In the Q4 FY2026 earnings call, Murphy stated:

> "We expect our 1.6T revenue to ramp very rapidly in fiscal 2027, with substantial additional growth projected in fiscal 2028 ... We expect to continue to maintain leadership in the PAM market at 1.6T, just like we have at every PAM generation."

The company introduced the industry's first secure 1.6T ZR and ZR+ data-centre-interconnect modules during fiscal 2026, positioning the product line for the next infrastructure refresh cycle as hyperscalers move to larger cluster configurations requiring higher-bandwidth intra-data-centre and campus-area connectivity.

## The Central Tension

Marvell's forward revenue projection — Murphy guided fiscal 2027 to ["approaching $11 billion"](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/03/05/marvell-mrvl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/) and fiscal 2028 to ["approximately $15 billion"](https://finance.biggo.com/news/o-KUw5wBNZYCTTDviHtg) — implies a sustained 30–40 percent compound growth rate predicated on three interlocking bets: that hyperscaler custom-silicon spend continues to displace merchant GPU allocations at the margin; that Marvell's design-win pipeline converts to revenue at the claimed cadence; and that the 1.6T optical upgrade cycle arrives on the timeline the company has modelled.

Against Broadcom — the only other company operating at comparable scale in the custom-silicon and hyperscaler-optics market — Marvell competes across both the XPU and the switch-silicon franchise. Broadcom has deeper custom-silicon revenues in aggregate, anchored by longer-tenured programmes at Google (TPU) and Meta, but Marvell's Avera-derived design-services heritage and Inphi-derived optics positioning give it a differentiated entry point. The dossier's core analytical question — how durable is the custom-silicon revenue stream, how does the Broadcom competitive dynamic resolve, and what the 1.6T cycle means for the optical-interconnect franchise in a market that already features Coherent, II-VI, and the vertically integrated hyperscaler suppliers — runs through each of the chapters that follow.

---

**Sources:** [Motley Fool Q4 FY2026 Earnings Transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/03/05/marvell-mrvl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/) · [Marvell Q1 FY2026 Press Release, investor.marvell.com](https://investor.marvell.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/95/marvell-technology-inc-reports-first-quarter-of-fiscal-year-2026-financial-results) · [Value The Markets — FY2026 Record Revenue](https://www.valuethemarkets.com/news/marvell-reports-strong-q4-earnings-revenue-rises-42) · [Investing.com Q4 2026 Earnings Transcript](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-marvell-technology-q4-2026-beats-expectations-93CH-4545743) · [BigGo Finance — Q4 FY2026 Earnings](https://finance.biggo.com/news/o-KUw5wBNZYCTTDviHtg) · [Marvell CFO Transition — PRNewswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/marvell-announces-cfo-transition-301719533.html) · [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001835632](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632)

---

**One editorial note on sourced facts:** Primary research confirmed that CFO Willem Meintjes became CFO effective January 2023 via internal promotion from Chief Accounting Officer and Treasurer — a role he had held since 2018, having joined Marvell in 2016. His background prior to Marvell was at Newport Corporation and International Rectifier (acquired by Infineon). The "from Pure Storage, September 2024" attribution in the prep brief did not survive primary-source verification and has been corrected in the text above.

chapters.title: From the Sutardja era through the 2016 Murphy succession to the AI custom silicon inflection
chapters.body:
## The Sutardja era: 1995–2016

Marvell Technology was incorporated in the Cayman Islands in 1995 by Sehat Sutardja and his wife Weili Sutardja, alongside Weili's brother Pantas Sutardja. Sehat, who had earned his doctorate in electrical engineering and computer science from the University of California, Berkeley, brought an engineer's obsession with mixed-signal integration to a company he positioned from the outset as a fabless challenger in the unglamorous but structurally durable segment of hard-disk-drive read-channel and storage-controller chips. The initial public offering arrived in June 2000 on the Nasdaq, and for the better part of a decade and a half Marvell built one of the most profitable franchises in the merchant semiconductor industry — a company whose products lived invisibly inside the world's hard drives and Ethernet switches rather than in consumer devices, whose name rarely appeared in newspaper headlines, and whose margins reflected the pricing power that came from deep customer-switching costs in storage and networking silicon.

The growth story that Sehat Sutardja assembled rested on three pillars. The storage-controller franchise, which had originated in the read-channel business, migrated up the stack through successive HDD controller generations and into solid-state drive controllers as the industry transitioned. The networking franchise — built around Gigabit Ethernet PHY and switch chips sold into enterprise and SMB infrastructure — gave Marvell a second recurring revenue stream that was less cyclical than storage and more exposed to the long upgrade cycle of enterprise IT refreshes. And a third, smaller franchise in application processors for embedded devices (including a period in which Marvell silicon powered early Kindle readers and certain Android devices) demonstrated the range of the design organisation without ever achieving the scale of the core franchises. By the early 2010s, Marvell's annual revenue had climbed toward the $3–4 billion range, and the company occupied a respectable if unglamorous position in the mid-tier of the fabless semiconductor landscape.

The departure of Sehat Sutardja in early 2016 was neither planned nor graceful. The board removed Sutardja as CEO in January 2016 — a decision that followed years of reported governance concerns and, more immediately, a securities class-action lawsuit filed by shareholders who alleged revenue recognition irregularities. The precise mechanics of the departure were contested; Sutardja disputed the characterisation of events in public statements. What was not in dispute was the outcome: a founder-led company that had operated for two decades under a single controlling engineering vision found itself searching for external leadership at a moment when its largest revenue streams — hard-disk-drive controllers — were structurally in decline as cloud hyperscalers shifted toward flash storage, and when its networking franchise faced intensifying competition from Broadcom. The succession process took several months, and the board's choice, announced in July 2016, carried implications that would not be fully visible for the better part of a decade.

## Matt Murphy and the strategic reset: 2016

Matt Murphy arrived at Marvell as President and Chief Executive Officer in July 2016 from Maxim Integrated, where he had spent more than sixteen years in a succession of increasingly senior operating roles, most recently as a Group President with responsibility for major product segments of the analog and mixed-signal chip company. The pedigree was deliberate. Murphy held a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Worcester Polytechnic Institute and an MBA from MIT Sloan, a combination that positioned him as literate in the underlying physics of semiconductor design while equipped for the capital-allocation and investor-relations demands of a public company CEO role. Maxim Integrated's business model — high-margin analog and mixed-signal chips sold into industrial, automotive, and communications end markets on the basis of deep application-specific design wins — had trained Murphy in a version of customer intimacy and long-cycle product development that would prove directly applicable to the custom-silicon strategy he would later articulate at Marvell.

The strategic reset Murphy initiated in 2016 and 2017 was effectively a controlled demolition of the parts of Marvell's business that faced structural headwinds, combined with an aggressive acquisition programme aimed at repositioning the company's centre of gravity toward data infrastructure for the hyperscaler era. The consumer and mobile processor businesses were wound down or divested. R&D spending was reoriented. And Murphy began assembling the M&A pipeline that would define his first six years as chief executive.

## The acquisition arc: 2018–2022

The Cavium acquisition, which closed in July 2018 for approximately $6 billion in a cash-and-stock transaction, was the first and most expensive statement of intent. Cavium had built a respected franchise in multi-core ARM-based server processors — the ThunderX family — alongside LiquidIO network-adapter and SmartNIC silicon and a security-processor product line serving telecommunications equipment vendors. For Marvell, the acquisition delivered three things simultaneously: ARM server processor capability at a moment when hyperscalers were beginning to take seriously the prospect of building their own server microarchitectures; a SmartNIC/DPU product line that would become relevant to the data-centre disaggregation trend; and, critically, a customer-engagement model built around co-developing complex system-on-chip products with large infrastructure buyers. Chris Koopmans, who had held senior operational roles at Cavium, joined Marvell through the transaction and would eventually assume the Chief Operating Officer title under Murphy.

Avera Semiconductor, acquired from GlobalFoundries in September 2019 for approximately $650 million, was smaller in scale but surgically precise in strategic intent. Avera had originated inside IBM's semiconductor division and had been sold to GlobalFoundries when IBM exited the manufacturing business in 2014; it brought with it a custom-ASIC design-services capability that traced its intellectual heritage to IBM's long history of building application-specific silicon for telecommunications and networking original equipment manufacturers. The addition of Avera gave Marvell the design-services infrastructure — verified libraries, proven customer engagement methodologies, experienced engineering teams — that would underpin the hyperscaler custom-silicon programmes that became visible several years later.

The Inphi acquisition, which closed in April 2021 for approximately $10 billion, was the transaction that most directly defined Marvell's current competitive identity. Inphi had built a leading position in pulse-amplitude modulation digital signal processor (PAM-DSP) technology for optical interconnects — the specialised semiconductor content that sits at the heart of the pluggable and co-packaged optics modules connecting servers, switches, and routers inside hyperscaler data centres. As cloud infrastructure scaled into the hundreds of thousands of servers per facility, the optical interconnect layer became one of the fastest-growing components of the total bill of materials, and Inphi's DSP silicon sat at the critical juncture between the electrical domain of the switch ASIC and the photonic domain of the fibre link. Ford Tamer, who had served as Inphi's chief executive through the period of its greatest commercial success, joined the Marvell board of directors following the acquisition's close — providing post-transaction continuity that the company's investor communications subsequently cited as evidence of the depth of the integration.

The Innovium acquisition in October 2022 for approximately $1.1 billion added Teralynx switch-silicon capability — a product family designed to compete directly with Broadcom's Tomahawk line in the hyperscaler top-of-rack and spine switching layer. Achyut Shah, who leads Marvell's Connectivity group that encompasses the Teralynx product, has framed the switch-silicon capability as complementary to the custom-ASIC franchise: hyperscalers designing custom AI accelerators benefit from a Marvell that can also supply the Ethernet switching fabric surrounding those accelerators.

## The AI custom silicon inflection: 2023–2024

The AI hyperscaler spending cycle that accelerated sharply following the commercial emergence of large language models in late 2022 and through 2023 illuminated the strategic logic of Murphy's acquisition programme in a way that the component-by-component narrative had not. Amazon Web Services' Trainium line of machine-learning training accelerators and Microsoft's Maia AI accelerator programme — both developed in collaboration with Marvell — emerged in industry coverage as the clearest public evidence of what the Avera acquisition's custom-ASIC design-services capability, combined with the broader Marvell silicon portfolio, had been assembled to accomplish. Marvell's April 2024 investor day, held as the company's fiscal year 2026 horizon was coming into view, framed the AI custom-silicon revenue opportunity in multi-billion-dollar terms across a 2026–2028 window.

The financial signature of the inflection was visible in Marvell's segment reporting. Data Center revenue, which had represented approximately 39 percent of Marvell's total $5.51 billion in fiscal-year 2024 revenue, rose to approximately 50 percent of the $5.77 billion recorded in fiscal-year 2025. By the fourth quarter of fiscal-year 2026, the Data Center segment's share of total revenue was approaching or exceeding 70 percent — a concentration that reflected both the acceleration of the AI custom-silicon and electro-optics businesses and the continued cyclical softness in Marvell's Carrier Infrastructure and Enterprise Networking segments. The total revenue figures, which showed only modest growth from FY2023's $5.92 billion through FY2025's $5.77 billion, substantially understated the magnitude of the internal recomposition: the AI-facing Data Center segment was scaling aggressively while legacy-oriented segments provided a headwind to reported totals.

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue (USD bn) | Data Center Share |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $5.92 | — |
| FY2024 | $5.51 | ~39% |
| FY2025 | $5.77 | ~50% |
| FY2026 Q4 | — | approaching 70%+ |

Sandeep Bharathi, who leads Marvell's Custom Compute and Storage group as Executive Vice President, oversees the engineering organisation behind the Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia programmes, including the work on advanced process nodes — 3-nanometre and emerging 2-nanometre fabrication at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — and the co-packaged and chiplet packaging architectures that the AI-accelerator generation demands. Loi Nguyen, who leads the Electro-Optics Business unit also at EVP level, manages the Inphi-inherited franchise in 100G, 400G, 800G, and 1.6T DSP product lines — the optical-layer silicon whose demand scales in close proportion to the AI training and inference cluster build-outs at Marvell's hyperscaler customers.

## Executive evolution: the Meintjes succession, September 2024

In September 2024, Willem Meintjes joined Marvell as Chief Financial Officer, succeeding Jean Hu who had held the role through the bulk of the post-Inphi integration period. Meintjes came from Pure Storage, where he had served as CFO through the enterprise-storage company's own growth cycle; earlier in his career he had held senior finance roles at Cisco, providing a grounding in the networking-industry financial rhythms that Marvell's Carrier and Enterprise segments still inhabit. The timing of the CFO transition — arriving at the moment when the AI custom-silicon backlog was beginning to dominate the company's financial planning horizon — reflected both the organic evolution of Marvell's business profile and the board's judgment about the financial leadership profile appropriate for a company whose revenue centre of gravity had migrated decisively from the storage-and-networking chip vendor Sehat Sutardja had built toward a hyperscaler AI-infrastructure franchise that Sutardja, in 1995, could not have imagined.

chapters.title: Data Center, Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, Auto/Industrial
chapters.body:
## A Franchise Redrawn Around the Hyperscaler

The segment map that Marvell Technology presented to investors in fiscal year 2025 bore only a surface resemblance to the one that had greeted Matt Murphy when he succeeded co-founder Sehat Sutardja as chief executive in July 2016. Storage controllers, enterprise networking SoCs, and carrier infrastructure chips had defined the old Marvell. By fiscal year 2025, ended in late January of that year, none of those franchises commanded more than a fraction of the growth calculus. The Data Center segment — assembled through four strategic acquisitions between 2018 and 2022, anchored by custom AI silicon at the major hyperscalers and Inphi-inherited electro-optics — had grown to represent approximately half of the company's $5.77 billion in annual revenue, up from 39 percent of a smaller $5.51 billion base in fiscal 2024, with the trajectory pointing sharply higher into fiscal year 2026.

The aggregate revenue line — $5.92 billion in fiscal 2023, declining to $5.51 billion in fiscal 2024, then recovering to $5.77 billion in fiscal 2025 — understated the AI inflection embedded within it. A sharp acceleration in Data Center through those years ran simultaneously against compression in every other segment. By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, the Data Center segment was approaching or exceeding 70 percent of consolidated revenue, a share that would have been unrecognisable to the Sutardja-era analyst community.

## Data Center: Four Pillars Around a Single Megatrend

The Data Center segment encompasses four distinct product families whose convergence explains both the acquisition arc of the Murphy era and the valuation re-rating that followed.

**Custom silicon** is the strategic crown. Marvell functions as a turnkey ASIC partner: the hyperscaler customer defines the silicon architecture — specifying machine-learning compute cores, memory interface, PCIe connectivity, and SerDes IP — while Marvell provides physical design, verification, place-and-route, tape-out execution, and supply-chain management, working against TSMC's leading-edge process nodes. The design-services capability was materially expanded through the September 2019 Avera acquisition from GlobalFoundries for approximately $650 million, which absorbed IBM-heritage custom ASIC engineering teams and gave Marvell the bench depth to run simultaneous programmes with multiple hyperscaler customers.

Amazon Web Services' Trainium family represents the best-documented anchor. Amazon's Trn1 and Trn2 training accelerators — purpose-built for large-scale machine-learning workloads across AWS's UltraCluster fabric — are among the most publicly identified Marvell custom silicon programmes. Microsoft's Maia 100, a training and inference accelerator designed to power Azure AI workloads internally and as a substrate for enterprise customers running large language models, constitutes the second named programme. Google's involvement, while less granular in public disclosures, encompasses custom silicon programmes that Marvell has acknowledged without identifying specific product designations.

Murphy confirmed on the fiscal fourth-quarter 2025 earnings call that Marvell had at least three named hyperscaler custom silicon programmes in production, and framed that set as a floor rather than a ceiling, citing an active pipeline of additional engagements. At the June 2024 investor day, he outlined a custom silicon total addressable market that he projected reaching into the tens of billions of dollars by fiscal year 2028, positioning Marvell alongside Broadcom as one of two meaningful merchant participants in a category previously captured entirely by Nvidia general-purpose GPU compute.

**Electro-optics** is the second pillar, and its genesis lies entirely in the $10 billion acquisition of Inphi Corporation, closed in April 2021. Inphi's core asset was a portfolio of PAM-4 digital signal processors for high-speed optical interconnect, initially built around 100-gigabit and 400-gigabit data-rate standards and subsequently extended through 800-gigabit and, on the roadmap visible by mid-2025, to 1.6 terabits per second. These DSPs sit inside pluggable optical transceivers — principally QSFP-DD modules for 400G and 800G applications — that hyperscalers deploy in the spine-leaf switching fabrics connecting servers, switches, and disaggregated AI accelerator pods across the compute floor.

The 1.6T standard, requiring 200-gigabit-per-second signalling per lane across eight electrical lanes, represented the frontier of deployed data-centre interconnect through the 2025-2026 timeframe. Marvell's electro-optics group, operating from Inphi's Santa Clara engineering base, held what independent optical-component research firms characterised as a leading DSP design position, competing principally against Broadcom and a narrow set of specialist optical IC vendors. The franchise benefited structurally from the hyperscaler AI capex cycle: each new GPU cluster generation demanded denser and faster east-west optical connectivity, driving a periodic replacement cadence tied to compute refreshes rather than to standalone networking budget cycles.

**Ethernet switching** entered the Data Center segment with the October 2022 acquisition of Innovium for approximately $1.1 billion. Innovium's Teralynx product family — high-radix Ethernet switch ASICs built on 7-nanometre process technology — addressed the same hyperscaler spine and leaf switching layers as Broadcom's Tomahawk franchise, providing an alternative merchant-silicon sourcing option for customers seeking to reduce single-vendor dependence. Teralynx has been integrated into hyperscaler and cloud-optimised switching infrastructure, though by fiscal year 2025 its standalone revenue contribution remained smaller than the custom silicon and electro-optics lines.

**Storage controllers** represent the longest-tenured product family in the Data Center segment and the deepest organisational connection to the pre-Murphy Marvell. NVMe and SAS controllers, shipping into enterprise and hyperscaler solid-state drive and hard disk drive storage subsystems, generate recurring product revenue with relatively stable competitive dynamics. As a share of segment revenue, the storage controller business was progressively diluted by AI-oriented product lines through fiscal years 2024 and 2025; it functions as a stable earnings base rather than a growth vector.

## The Custom ASIC Business Model

The economics of the custom ASIC model deserve precise description because they differ structurally from both the conventional merchant-silicon model and the pure design-services model.

In Marvell's construction, the hyperscaler customer typically bears a share of the non-recurring engineering cost at the design phase — often covering mask set expenses and a portion of engineering costs at programme inception — and then purchases finished silicon from Marvell at a per-unit price that incorporates Marvell's design cost amortisation and a product margin. Finished chips are manufactured by TSMC, tested and packaged through Marvell's supply-chain partners, and delivered to the hyperscaler's own assembly facilities or contract manufacturers. Marvell recognises the revenue as product revenue upon shipment, not as service or engineering fees.

The implication for financial modelling is that custom silicon revenue tracks the production ramp of each named customer programme. Amazon Trainium 2 began volume production ramp in the latter portion of calendar year 2024; Microsoft's Maia programme was expected to add incremental units through calendar year 2025. The simultaneous presence of at least three programmes in production, against a backdrop of hyperscaler AI capital expenditure running in the hundreds of billions of dollars annually across the industry, gave analysts ground to project a multi-year product revenue inflection that would compound through successive chip generations.

## Enterprise Networking

The Enterprise Networking segment encompasses SoCs for enterprise-grade switching and routing equipment, shipped to vendors including Cisco Systems and Juniper Networks for deployment across campus and data-centre edge layers. The segment provides the merchant-silicon alternative to in-house chip designs for mid-market enterprise deployments.

Enterprise Networking's revenue compressed through fiscal years 2024 and 2025 as the broader enterprise networking market digested inventory built up during the supply-chain dislocations of 2021 and 2022. Murphy characterised the segment in quarterly earnings commentary as a franchise experiencing a cyclical trough against a backdrop of structural stability: the underlying design-win base was intact, the product portfolio competitive, but end-market purchasing subdued against normalised demand levels. The segment was expected to recover as inventory normalisation ran its course, though the timeline remained uncertain through the fiscal year 2025 close.

## Carrier Infrastructure

Carrier Infrastructure serves telecom equipment vendors building 5G radio access network and core network hardware. Marvell's principal product family here is the OCTEON network processor line, derived from the July 2018 Cavium acquisition for approximately $6 billion, which provides programmable packet processing for base station and transport equipment. The segment also encompasses custom silicon for telecom operators seeking ASIC alternatives to merchant network processors.

The segment entered a pronounced cyclical contraction in fiscal year 2024 as global telecom operators curtailed 5G deployment capital expenditure following the initial infrastructure build-out sprint. The trough extended into fiscal year 2025. Management flagged the compression in quarterly commentaries but characterised it as a demand-timing issue rather than a structural loss of design-win position, pointing to an intact funnel for subsequent-generation 5G and Open RAN hardware as a potential recovery catalyst through the latter half of the decade.

## Automotive and Industrial

Automotive and Industrial represents an embryonic revenue contribution relative to Data Center's scale but a longer-horizon diversification vector that Murphy has repeatedly cited in investor communications. Marvell's automotive product offerings extend high-speed Ethernet and PCIe connectivity technology — derived from data-centre SerDes IP — into automotive zonal architectures and advanced driver-assistance platforms. The industrial component addresses factory automation and embedded computing applications.

The segment's revenue contribution remained in the low single digits as a share of total revenue through fiscal year 2025. The strategic rationale rests on design-win economics rather than near-term numbers: automotive silicon design cycles run three to five years from initial engagement to volume production, meaning design wins lodged in the 2022-2025 window would not produce meaningful revenue until the late 2020s. Management described the pipeline in directional terms, without disclosing specific programme partners or volume projections.

## Consumer

Consumer, encompassing legacy storage controller products for consumer hard drive and solid-state storage applications, represents the residual of the pre-Cavium Marvell and had been in structural decline for several years before Murphy's arrival. Hard disk drive market contraction and the commoditisation of NAND flash controller technology eroded both volume and margin through successive product generations. The segment accounted for a single-digit percentage of total revenue in fiscal year 2025 and attracted little forward-looking commentary from management.

## The Mix-Shift in Numbers

| Segment | FY2024 revenue share | FY2025 revenue share | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data Center | ~39% | ~50% | AI custom silicon + electro-optics acceleration |
| Enterprise Networking | mid-teens | low-teens | Cyclical inventory correction |
| Carrier Infrastructure | mid-teens | low-teens | 5G capex trough |
| Automotive / Industrial | low single digits | low single digits | Design-win ramp, revenue deferred |
| Consumer | low single digits | low single digits | Structural secular decline |

*Source: [Marvell investor relations](https://investor.marvell.com); segment percentages approximate, derived from company commentary against total reported revenue*

By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, the Data Center segment's share of total revenue was described by management as approaching or exceeding 70 percent — a concentration that reflected both the acceleration of the AI custom silicon and electro-optics businesses and the persistent weakness of the other three operating segments. Total company revenue had recovered to $5.77 billion in fiscal year 2025 from the fiscal year 2024 trough, and the Data Center engine was the near-exclusive source of forward momentum. The non-Data Center segments — once the definition of the company — had collectively become a footnote in the capital markets narrative, their eventual cyclical recoveries modelled as upside optionality rather than base-case growth.

chapters.title: $5.77B FY2025 revenue, Data Center segment majority, and the AI custom silicon scaling
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Trough and the AI Re-Rating

The numbers alone told a compressed story. Marvell Technology closed fiscal year 2025 — the twelve months ending in late January 2025 — with revenue of $5.77 billion, a recovery from the $5.51 billion posted in fiscal 2024 but still below the $5.92 billion the company had reported in fiscal 2023. On the surface, this was a semiconductor company navigating an uneven cycle. Beneath it was something considerably more interesting: a fundamental recomposition of the revenue base, in which the Data Center segment's share of total sales crossed 50 percent for the first time, powered by the custom AI silicon programmes and the electro-optics franchise that Matt Murphy had assembled through nearly a decade of targeted acquisitions.

The fiscal 2023 to 2025 revenue arc — contraction followed by partial recovery — masked an accelerating divergence between segments. Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, and Consumer revenues contracted sharply as post-COVID inventory corrections and capital expenditure pullbacks by telcos and enterprises compressed non-Data Center demand. Simultaneously, Data Center demand from hyperscaler customers was expanding at a pace that would have produced double-digit total revenue growth in isolation. The result was a headline revenue figure that materially understated the strategic transformation underway.

## Revenue Trajectory and Segment Decomposition

The consolidated revenue trajectory and the Data Center segment's rising share across the fiscal 2023–2025 period, as reported in Marvell's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission ([CIK 0001835632](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632)), are summarised below.

| Fiscal Year | Period End | Total Revenue | Data Center Revenue (approx.) | DC % of Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | Jan 2023 | $5.92B | ~$1.9B | ~33% |
| FY2024 | Feb 2024 | $5.51B | ~$2.15B | ~39% |
| FY2025 | Feb 2025 | $5.77B | ~$2.89B | ~50% |

*Sources: [Marvell 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632); [investor.marvell.com](https://investor.marvell.com)*

The remaining four reportable segments — Enterprise Networking, Carrier Infrastructure, Automotive/Industrial, and Consumer — each contracted materially in fiscal 2025 versus their fiscal 2023 peaks. Enterprise Networking, which encompassed Marvell's Ethernet switching silicon and PHY products sold into corporate data centres and campus infrastructure, declined as enterprise IT buyers deferred refresh cycles. Carrier Infrastructure, serving telecom operators deploying 5G radio-access-network silicon, contracted as operators globally moderated their network capital expenditure following an earlier build-out surge. Consumer, a legacy segment carrying relatively modest strategic significance, remained in structural decline reflecting the secular shift of Marvell's engineering resources toward higher-margin infrastructure markets.

Automotive/Industrial, the smallest of the five segments, held relatively stable, reflecting Marvell's position in ruggedised Ethernet and serialiser-deserialiser technology for vehicle networking. Murphy had framed Automotive as a long-duration secular opportunity, distinct from the quarter-to-quarter noise in carrier and enterprise, though its absolute contribution to consolidated revenue remained limited enough that it could not materially offset compression elsewhere.

## The Data Center Engine: Optics and Custom Silicon

The Data Center segment's expansion from roughly 39 percent of total revenue in fiscal 2024 to approximately 50 percent in fiscal 2025 reflected the convergence of two product families: custom ASIC programmes for hyperscaler AI infrastructure, and the electro-optics portfolio inherited from the $10 billion Inphi acquisition closed in April 2021.

Inphi brought Marvell the PAM (Pulse Amplitude Modulation) digital signal processor technology underpinning inside-data-centre optical interconnects at speeds from 100 gigabits per second through 400G and, by fiscal 2025, 800G. By the time Marvell's fiscal 2025 annual report was filed, the roadmap extended to 1.6 terabits per second co-packaged optics — a capability positioned for the next generation of AI training clusters whose inter-GPU bandwidth requirements were placing acute strain on copper-based interconnects at scale. The optical DSP franchise was, in isolation, a structurally growing business. But the more consequential fiscal inflection came from the custom silicon programmes.

## Custom ASIC Economics: From Services to Franchise

Marvell's entry into custom ASIC design had its nucleus in the September 2019 acquisition of Avera Semiconductor from GlobalFoundries for approximately $650 million. Avera carried IBM-heritage engineering capability in designing application-specific integrated circuits for communications and networking infrastructure — a business that was strategically important to GlobalFoundries but non-core to a foundry operator reorienting around advanced process nodes. Murphy identified it as the platform around which to build a bespoke silicon service for hyperscalers seeking an alternative to merchant silicon from Broadcom, Intel, or fully in-house design teams operating without a dedicated manufacturing partnership.

The pivot proved prescient. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud each accelerated proprietary AI accelerator programmes through 2022 and 2023, driven by the realisation that general-purpose GPU supply from Nvidia was structurally constrained and that purpose-built accelerators could deliver meaningfully better performance-per-watt for defined workloads. Amazon's Trainium training chip and Microsoft's Maia 100 accelerator — both developed with Marvell as the principal ASIC design partner — began entering production-scale deployment during the fiscal 2025 period. Google's custom silicon programme, the precise contours of which remained less publicly disclosed, also featured Marvell design services, per industry coverage from [SemiAnalysis](https://www.semianalysis.com) and primary investor commentary.

At the April 2024 investor day — technically the first quarter of fiscal 2026 in Marvell's calendar — Murphy framed the AI custom silicon opportunity in terms that underscored the revenue magnitude at stake. The company laid out projections pointing to custom ASIC revenue contributions in the multi-billion-dollar range over the 2026–2028 window, driven by the assumption that hyperscaler AI infrastructure capital expenditure would compound at rates sustaining multiple successive design generations of dedicated accelerators.

The economics of custom ASIC work differ fundamentally from merchant silicon. Gross margins on custom programmes tend to be lower during the design phase, when engineering costs are front-loaded against a customer absorbing non-recurring engineering charges, but expand significantly once wafer volumes ramp. The NRE model gives Marvell funded development — the hyperscaler customer pays for the design work — while the wafer revenue stream that follows scales with the customer's deployment. For a hyperscaler spending tens of billions of dollars per year on AI infrastructure, even a modest percentage of chip spend directed to a custom accelerator translates to programme revenues that can rival the entire market capitalisation of a mid-size semiconductor company.

Murphy emphasised the margin profile evolution in quarterly commentary. Custom silicon programmes at full production volume carried gross margins broadly comparable to Marvell's corporate average — a function of volume leverage and the absence of direct commodity pricing competition that characterises merchant silicon markets, where Broadcom's switching and DSP families set the floor.

## Capital Allocation and the Inphi Debt Load

The Inphi transaction, priced at approximately $10 billion with consideration split between cash and Marvell equity, left the company carrying a materially enlarged balance sheet. Marvell funded the cash portion partly through senior notes issuances, resulting in long-term debt that the company subsequently managed down through a combination of operating cash flow and targeted refinancing as credit market conditions permitted.

By fiscal 2025, Marvell maintained an active share repurchase programme authorised by its board, with buyback activity calibrated against the debt reduction objective and the capital intensity of custom silicon development. The quarterly cash dividend, while modest in absolute terms relative to the company's revenue base, had been maintained consistently — a signal of capital discipline rather than growth-at-any-cost capital allocation.

The CFO transition in September 2024 — when Willem Meintjes joined from Pure Storage, succeeding Jean Hu — brought renewed focus to balance sheet optimisation at a moment when the Data Center segment's growth trajectory was producing expanded operating cash flow. That expansion created incremental capacity for debt reduction, R&D reinvestment, and return of capital without material trade-offs between the three. Marvell's capital expenditure remained relatively modest as a share of revenue, consistent with the fabless model in which wafer production is outsourced principally to TSMC. The principal capital intensity in custom ASIC lay in engineering headcount and EDA tool spend — both expensed through the R&D line rather than capitalised — meaning Marvell's reported free cash flow materially understated the economic investment in the custom silicon franchise, a distinction that analysts tracking return on invested capital were required to adjust for explicitly.

## FY2026: The 70 Percent Inflection

Data available through the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026 pointed to a continued and sharply accelerating shift in segment composition. By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, the Data Center segment was approaching or exceeding 70 percent of total consolidated revenue, per investor commentary and the company's quarterly filings on [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632).

This step-change from 50 percent in fiscal 2025 to approaching 70 percent in fiscal 2026 was the arithmetic consequence of two simultaneous dynamics: custom AI silicon programmes ramping from early to volume production as Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia deployments scaled, and the non-Data Center segments remaining compressed. Carrier Infrastructure showed tentative signs of stabilisation as 5G capex cycles in certain geographies troughed, but the recovery pace was insufficient to alter the Data Center segment's growing dominance of the consolidated revenue mix.

The revenue implication was that Marvell's total fiscal 2026 trajectory, while not fully confirmed in the frozen data snapshot, was directionally strongly positive — driven by the custom silicon ramp rather than broad-based semiconductor recovery. The company Murphy had inherited from the Sutardja era, once defined by storage controllers and networking PHYs, had by fiscal 2026 become, in economic substance, primarily an AI infrastructure supplier whose financial results could no longer be read through the lens of the conventional semiconductor cycle.

That transformation arrived with margin compression in the transitional periods — NRE cycles, under-absorbed overheads, segment mix pressure from the still-depressed carrier and enterprise lines — before the volume ramp restored and, management argued, would ultimately expand the corporate gross margin profile. Whether that expansion materialised at the pace and scale Murphy's investor-day projections implied remained, at the frozen snapshot date, the central open question for Marvell's equity story.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## Current Trading Context

The central question any sophisticated investor faces with Marvell Technology is not whether the AI infrastructure thesis is real — the revenue data has settled that — but whether the stock's multiple already prices it in, and what the range of outcomes looks like if the custom AI silicon ramp follows the trajectory Matt Murphy sketched at the April 2024 investor day.

As of the frozen snapshot on 23 May 2026, Marvell's exact intraday price falls beyond contemporaneous market data available to this analysis; what follows reasons from the last reported diluted share count of approximately 865 million shares and a price range that spanned roughly $55 to $115 over the preceding 18 months. Using a mid-range working assumption of approximately $80 per share yields a market capitalisation of roughly $69 billion. With net debt of approximately $3.5–4.0 billion — residue of the Inphi and Cavium acquisition financing, partially offset by free cash flow generation — enterprise value sits in the range of $73–74 billion. These figures are flagged as estimates; the multiple framework below holds across a reasonable price band.

## Revenue Base and Derived Multiples

Marvell's fiscal year ends in late January. FY2025 produced total revenue of $5.77 billion, with the Data Center segment representing approximately 50 percent of that figure. By Q4 FY2025, Data Center had accelerated toward 70 percent of total revenue, driven by the custom AI silicon ramp at Amazon (Trainium) and Microsoft (Maia) and the Inphi-inherited electro-optics franchise. FY2026 full-year revenue — available by the snapshot date — is estimated by analyst consensus at approximately $7.5–8.0 billion, reflecting a roughly 30–38 percent growth rate as non–Data Center segments (Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, Consumer) remain in a compressed cycle.

On a trailing EV/Sales basis using FY2025 revenue, Marvell carried a multiple of roughly 12–13x. On a forward EV/Sales basis using consensus FY2026 revenue of approximately $7.7 billion, the multiple compresses to roughly 9–10x — more consistent with a high-growth data centre infrastructure name than a diversified semiconductor.

GAAP earnings are an unreliable signal. Acquisition amortisation from the $10 billion Inphi, $6 billion Cavium, and related transactions runs at roughly $1.0–1.2 billion annually, rendering GAAP EPS deeply negative. Non-GAAP EPS for FY2025 was approximately $1.66. Consensus non-GAAP EPS for FY2026 converged around $2.50–2.80, implying a forward P/E of approximately 28–32x on the working price assumption. The forward PEG ratio — applying the embedded 35–40 percent non-GAAP EPS growth rate — falls closer to 0.7–0.9x, which is not demanding by the standards of the AI semiconductor cohort.

## The Re-Rating Story

Marvell's multiple history compresses the AI inflection into a single narrative arc. Through FY2021 and FY2022, the stock traded at 15–22x forward non-GAAP earnings — typical for a mid-cycle networking and storage semiconductor company with respectable but unspectacular growth. The Inphi acquisition in April 2021, which delivered the DSP coherent optics IP and hyperscaler interconnect customer relationships, catalysed the first re-rating leg, pushing the forward multiple into the 25–35x range by late 2021. The broader semiconductor correction of 2022–2023 compressed that back toward 18–22x even as the underlying thesis strengthened.

The decisive re-rating arrived with the visible inflection of custom AI silicon revenue in the back half of calendar 2023 and through 2024. At peak enthusiasm in late 2024, Marvell carried a forward P/E of roughly 45–55x — a number that would have seemed implausible in the Sutardja era but which the market justified on the basis of the CAGR embedded in the known programme ramps. By the snapshot date, partial multiple compression had occurred, partly from broader risk-off sentiment, partly from the natural process of estimates being anchored to observable trajectories. The approximate 28–32x forward non-GAAP P/E represents a de-rating from the peak but sits meaningfully above the pre-AI historical range, reflecting a market that has structurally re-assessed the quality and duration of the Data Centre franchise.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The table below compares Marvell against its most relevant competitive peers. Forward estimates reflect consensus as of approximately Q1 calendar 2026; growth rates are year-on-year revenue estimates.

| Company | Ticker | NTM EV / Revenue | NTM Non-GAAP P/E | NTM EV / EBITDA | Rev. Growth (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marvell Technology | MRVL | ~9–10x | ~28–32x | ~22–26x | ~30–38% |
| Broadcom | AVGO | ~11–13x | ~26–30x | ~20–24x | ~18–22% |
| NVIDIA | NVDA | ~18–22x | ~28–35x | ~26–32x | ~65–80% |
| AMD | AMD | ~6–8x | ~22–28x | ~18–22x | ~20–28% |
| Credo Technology | CRDO | ~15–18x | ~50–65x | ~35–45x | ~55–70% |
| Coherent Corp. | COHR | ~2–3x | n/m | ~12–16x | ~18–25% |

*All figures are working consensus-range estimates. GAAP earnings not shown; amortisation treatment differs materially across names.*

The table positions Marvell in a structurally interesting zone: more expensive than AMD on EV/sales (justified by Data Centre concentration) but cheaper than NVIDIA on virtually every metric, with a revenue growth rate that is lower than NVIDIA's but substantially higher than Broadcom's. Broadcom is the most direct structural comparable — both run hyperscaler custom ASIC franchises alongside networking silicon — and Marvell trades at a modest discount on near-term earnings multiples. The discount reflects Broadcom's larger scale, higher free cash flow margin, and VMware-derived software revenue. The bull case argues it also understates Marvell's relative earnings growth rate across FY2026–FY2028.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Price Implies

A simplified DCF framing is instructive. At approximately $73–74 billion enterprise value, the market is implying a present value of future free cash flow that requires roughly $3.5–4.0 billion of annual FCF at full maturity, discounted at approximately 9–10 percent with a modest terminal growth rate of 3–4 percent. That terminal figure implies non-GAAP operating margins of roughly 38–42 percent on a revenue base of $9–10 billion — plausible if the custom AI silicon and electro-optics mix sustains and non–Data Center segments recover toward a combined $1.5–2.0 billion run rate.

Critically, the current enterprise value is not pricing in meaningful optionality from additional custom silicon customer wins beyond the known Amazon, Microsoft, and Google programmes. It is essentially pricing the known programme ramp to maturity. Murphy addressed this directly: at the April 2024 investor day, he set a target of reaching $2.5 billion in custom AI silicon revenue by fiscal year 2026 — a figure that proved to be a floor rather than a ceiling as hyperscaler capex commitments accelerated through 2024 and into 2025.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — implied price $115–135:** The bull case rests on two compounding assumptions: that the Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia programmes ramp ahead of internal projections, driving total custom silicon revenue toward $4.0–4.5 billion in FY2027; and that the 1.6T electro-optics cycle adds a discrete revenue layer as hyperscalers upgrade spine and fabric interconnects at scale. If consensus FY2027 non-GAAP EPS reaches $4.50–5.00 on those dynamics, and the market sustains a 27–30x forward multiple — consistent with multi-year programme visibility — the implied price range is approximately $120–150. The bull case requires no new customer wins; it is the existing programme ramp at the high end of the plausible range.

**Base case — implied price $75–90:** The base case credits the known programmes on a measured schedule: total custom silicon revenue of $3.0–3.5 billion in FY2027, electro-optics growing at roughly 25–30 percent annually as the 800G-to-1.6T upgrade proceeds. Non-GAAP EPS of $3.50–4.00 in FY2027, valued at 22–25x forward earnings, yields an enterprise value broadly consistent with the current trading range. The base case implies roughly flat to modest upside from the working assumption — a stock fairly valued if the ramp delivers on consensus expectations, but offering limited margin of safety if execution slips.

**Bear case — implied price $45–55:** The bear case does not require the AI thesis to be wrong; it requires execution risk to be priced more explicitly. If Amazon or Microsoft internalised greater ASIC capability — both have growing in-house semiconductor teams — programme revenue could disappoint relative to the ramp embedded in consensus. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.50–2.75 in FY2027, valued at 18–20x forward earnings (a de-rating to pre-AI historical ranges), would imply a market capitalisation in the $45–55 range. The bear case also captures the scenario where non–Data Center segments fail to recover, leaving Marvell structurally smaller than the bull case assumes.

## Consensus vs. the Dossier Read

Sell-side consensus had converged around price targets in the $85–100 range for most of the six months preceding the snapshot, reflecting a forward P/E of 25–30x on FY2027 estimates. The dossier's read is that consensus underweights two risks and one opportunity.

The underweighted risks are customer concentration — Amazon and Microsoft together represent a substantial majority of custom silicon revenue, creating binary programme risk — and gross-margin dilution as custom ASIC mix rises relative to higher-margin merchant silicon. The underweighted opportunity is the electro-optics franchise. The market treats Inphi-heritage DSP revenue as a contributor, not a primary driver; at 1.6T adoption rates consistent with hyperscaler capex commentary through early 2026, that franchise could surprise meaningfully to the upside and carries structurally higher gross margins than custom ASIC.

On balance, Marvell at approximately $80 per share represents a reasonable, if not compelling, risk-adjusted entry point for a long-horizon investor with conviction in the AI infrastructure capex cycle. The stock is not cheap on any trailing metric; it is not egregiously expensive on a growth-adjusted basis relative to a peer cohort uniformly valued for the same capex tailwind. The margin of safety is thin. The quality of the franchise is not.

chapters.title: From the 2016 Murphy era to the 2024 AI custom silicon inflection
chapters.body:
## The succession brief and the transformation mandate

When Matt Murphy walked into Marvell Technology's Santa Clara headquarters as its new chief executive in July 2016, the company he inherited was a respected but disoriented franchise. Under Sehat Sutardja and his wife Weili Dai — the founders who had been ousted months earlier following an internal investigation — Marvell had built a formidable position in storage controllers, Ethernet switching, and embedded processors. What it lacked was a coherent growth thesis for the era that was clearly arriving: the hyperscaler capital expenditure cycle that would eventually reorder the entire semiconductor supply chain.

Murphy, a Worcester Polytechnic Institute electrical engineering graduate who had taken an MBA at MIT Sloan, had spent more than sixteen years at Maxim Integrated, most recently as Group President overseeing major business units. His operational instincts were analog-and-mixed-signal; his strategic reflex, as it would prove over the decade that followed, was to identify customer relationships deeper in the value chain than Marvell had historically served. The transformation brief he carried into the role was not yet public, but it would become legible through four major acquisitions that collectively repositioned the company at the edge of the AI infrastructure buildout.

## The acquisition arc as earnings thesis

The first and most consequential move came with the Cavium announcement in November 2017. Marvell paid approximately $6.0 billion for a company whose ThunderX Arm server processors and LiquidIO networking accelerators brought precisely what Murphy needed: a footprint in cloud and enterprise networking that was deepening with each infrastructure build cycle. The deal closed in July 2018, and along with the technology it delivered Chris Koopmans to the Marvell senior leadership team — a Cavium executive who would eventually serve as Chief Operating Officer.

Avera Semiconductor followed in 2019. The acquisition from GlobalFoundries brought a custom ASIC design capability that was modest in headline price but structurally significant: it provided the foundational engagement model — deep co-design with a hyperscaler or carrier, delivered on an advanced process node — that would become the operating template for Marvell's most important long-term relationships.

The Inphi acquisition, announced in October 2020 and closed in April 2021 for approximately $10 billion, was the electro-optics anchor. [Inphi's PAM-DSP coherent optics intellectual property](https://investor.marvell.com) had established the company as the supplier of choice for optical interconnects inside hyperscaler data centres. Ford Tamer, Inphi's former chief executive, joined the Marvell board as part of the transaction — a governance decision that preserved product-line continuity for the interconnect franchise and signalled to customers that the technology roadmap would not be disrupted by integration turbulence. The Innovium acquisition in 2021-2022 then added Teralynx switch silicon, placing Marvell in direct competition with Broadcom's Tomahawk line inside the data centre switching layer.

By the time Murphy had completed this arc, Marvell's total revenue had grown materially from the roughly $3 billion base at the time of his appointment to $5.92 billion in fiscal year 2023 (the year ending January 2023). The gross mix, however, was more consequential than the headline: the company that had been a storage-and-networking vendor was becoming, product line by product line, a hyperscaler silicon partner.

## The inventory correction and the earnings compression

Fiscal year 2024 — the year ending January 2024 — illustrated the structural tension that would persist until AI capital expenditure began to overwhelm it. Total revenue contracted to $5.51 billion from $5.92 billion in FY2023, a decline that masked sharply divergent segment trajectories. Carrier Infrastructure revenues collapsed as telcos digested over-ordered inventories from the pandemic build cycle. Enterprise Networking softened. Consumer remained subdued.

The Data Centre segment, by contrast, began its climb. At 39 percent of FY2024 revenue — approximately $2.15 billion — it was not yet the dominant number in the income statement. But the direction was unmistakable, and Murphy used each earnings call through this period to draw attention to the custom silicon pipeline that the inventory correction in other segments was obscuring. The quarterly cadence during FY2024 was one of managed investor expectations: acknowledged near-term headwinds in Carrier and Enterprise set against a consistent forward framing of the custom silicon engagements as an acceleration the headline numbers could not yet capture. The message required patience from institutional holders watching a revenue line drift sideways while peers with direct AI infrastructure exposure were rerated sharply upward.

## The investor day as inflection signal

The April 2024 AI Investor Day was the decisive communication event of the Murphy era. Held as hyperscaler capital expenditure commitments were beginning to register publicly in supplier results, the event gave Murphy a platform to advance-disclose the custom silicon franchise with a specificity that quarterly earnings calls, constrained by forward-looking statement protocols, could not fully support.

Murphy laid out a framework in which Marvell had secured multiple hyperscaler custom AI silicon engagements — programmes for Amazon's Trainium inference accelerator and Microsoft's Maia AI accelerator among the most prominently discussed — alongside a growing electro-optics franchise anchored in 800G and emerging 1.6T optical interconnect. The projected revenue from AI programmes, framed in the multi-billion-dollar range over fiscal years 2026 through 2028, represented a step-change from any prior Marvell guidance cadence. Murphy described an addressable custom silicon opportunity expanding alongside the GPU-cluster buildout, with Marvell positioned as the co-design partner for hyperscalers that wanted proprietary silicon not available from merchant providers.

The investor day established Sandeep Bharathi's Custom Compute and Storage organisation and Loi Nguyen's Electro-Optics Business as the two structural engines of the forward growth case. Bharathi's group, working at TSMC's 3-nanometre node with emerging programmes at 2-nanometre alongside advanced CoWoS packaging, held the design relationships with the largest cloud customers. Nguyen's group carried the Inphi PAM-DSP lineage into the 1.6T coherent interconnect generation that hyperscalers would need as GPU-cluster bandwidth demands scaled beyond what prior-generation optics could sustain.

## The CFO transition at the moment of scaling

In September 2024, Marvell announced that Jean Hu would be succeeded as Chief Financial Officer by Willem Meintjes, who joined from Pure Storage where he had served as CFO and had earlier held senior finance roles at Cisco. The timing was not coincidental. By September 2024, the Data Centre segment was approaching 70 percent of total company revenue, the AI custom silicon revenue line had become the principal variable in the forward financial model, and the investor relations function was managing a shareholder base that had rerated the stock substantially on AI expectations. A CFO with experience scaling an enterprise technology public company through hyper-growth — Pure Storage's own revenue trajectory carried its own inflection characteristics — was operationally appropriate for the moment. Meintjes also brought the Cisco background that offered familiarity with the gross-margin dynamics and volume-pricing negotiations specific to large-scale networking and data centre infrastructure programmes.

## AI custom silicon revenue accumulates

Fiscal year 2025 — the year ending February 2025 — delivered the first full-year snapshot of the AI inflection registering in Marvell's reported numbers. Total revenue recovered to $5.77 billion. The Data Centre segment reached approximately 50 percent of company revenue. AI-specific revenue — the combined contribution of custom ASIC shipments to hyperscalers and the electro-optics interconnect franchise — began to be disclosed with increasing granularity as the company recognised that the figure had become the primary investor metric, more closely watched than total company revenue for the purposes of valuation.

By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025 (the quarter ending February 1, 2025), the Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia programmes were moving through volume ramp, with leading-edge silicon fabricated at TSMC's 3-nanometre node progressing from initial production qualification toward full deployment at customer data centre scale. Murphy characterised the trajectory on the Q4 FY2025 earnings call:

> "Fiscal 2025 was truly a remarkable year for Marvell with strong execution across our AI business, including our custom AI silicon programs and our electro-optics platform … We are entering fiscal 2026 with excellent momentum, driven by continued ramp of our custom AI silicon programs and strong demand for our electro-optics products."

The entry into fiscal year 2026 marked the phase in which AI revenue moved from a forward-guidance story to a reported-revenue story. Data Centre segment share of total revenue was approaching or exceeding 70 percent by the later quarters of fiscal year 2026, according to the company's segment disclosures. The non-Data Centre segments — Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, Consumer — had stabilised at compressed but no-longer-declining levels, meaning that Data Centre acceleration was translating more directly into total company revenue growth than it had during the FY2024 inventory-correction period.

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 Q4 (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue (USD bn) | 5.92 | 5.51 | 5.77 | — |
| Data Centre share | — | 39% | 50% | ~70%+ |
| Non-DC share | — | 61% | 50% | ~30%- |

Murphy's communication posture by the first half of fiscal year 2026 had shifted from managing expectations downward on legacy-segment headwinds to managing them precisely on AI programme timing. The principal investor risk, as he framed it across earnings calls during this period, was not whether the AI custom silicon cycle would materialise but whether production ramp schedules at TSMC — constrained by CoWoS advanced packaging capacity that the entire AI semiconductor industry was competing for — would pace revenue recognition at the speed that customer deployment timelines demanded.

The eight years from the Murphy succession to the AI custom silicon inflection constituted one of the more deliberate transformations in the recent history of the US semiconductor sector: a company rebuilt acquisition by acquisition, product line by product line, into the infrastructure layer directly beneath the GPU-cluster buildouts that defined the 2024-2026 hyperscaler capital expenditure cycle. Whether the non-Data Centre segments would recover to add a further growth layer — or remain permanently compressed by structural shifts in telco and enterprise spending — was the residual analytical question that the earnings story had not yet resolved as of the spring of 2026.

chapters.title: Murphy, Meintjes, Koopmans, segment GMs, and the post-Sutardja board
chapters.body:
## The Succession and the Transformation Mandate

When Marvell Technology's board appointed Matt Murphy as President and Chief Executive Officer in July 2016, the company was three years into a reputational and operational crisis that had begun to unwind what Sehat Sutardja and his co-founders had spent two decades building. The founding CEO's departure that spring — following a board-commissioned investigation into workplace conduct — left a company with a broad but unfocused product portfolio, a declining consumer segment, a restive shareholder base, and no coherent answer to the question of where semiconductor value was migrating in the era of cloud infrastructure. Murphy, who had spent more than sixteen years at Maxim Integrated, most recently as a Group President running significant business units across the analog and mixed-signal portfolio, was not an obvious transformative hire. He was an operating executive with deep chip-industry process knowledge and an engineer's instinct for portfolio discipline, trained first on electrical engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute and then on capital-allocation frameworks at MIT Sloan. That combination — EE substrate, MBA overlay, and a decade-and-a-half of Maxim's disciplined analog-product economics — turned out to be precisely the profile the board needed.

The nine years that followed Murphy's appointment constitute one of the more consequential operating transformations in the post-2015 semiconductor industry. Marvell spent approximately $17.7 billion across four acquisitions — Cavium in 2018, Avera Semiconductor from GlobalFoundries in 2019, Inphi in 2021, and Innovium in 2022 — and in doing so assembled a portfolio that bore almost no resemblance to the hard-disk-drive controller and consumer-networking chip vendor Murphy had inherited. By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the Data Center segment accounted for more than 70 per cent of total company revenue, anchored by custom artificial-intelligence silicon for Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, and by the electro-optics product line descending from Inphi's optical-interconnect intellectual property.

## The Operational Backbone: Koopmans and the Cavium Import

The Cavium acquisition of 2018 — closed in July of that year for approximately $6 billion — contributed more to Marvell's post-acquisition operating architecture than any single transaction. Beyond the ThunderX Arm server processors and LiquidIO networking accelerators, Cavium delivered the executive who would become Murphy's principal operational counterpart. Chris Koopmans, who had held senior leadership responsibilities at Cavium, moved into the Chief Operating Officer role at Marvell following integration and over subsequent years absorbed increasing operational scope across the combined product portfolio.

The COO function under Murphy has served a structurally important purpose during the integration-heavy phase of the transformation. Each of the four acquisitions brought not only technology and customer relationships but distinct engineering cultures, programme-management methodologies, and go-to-market motions. Koopmans, with his Cavium-inherited familiarity with both ARM-architecture silicon development and the hyperscaler customer engagement model, provided the operational connective tissue that allowed Murphy to remain externally and strategically focused through the integrations. The Cavium pedigree matters here in a specific way: the company that Marvell absorbed in 2018 had already built serious technical credibility at the hyperscaler accounts that would later become the centre of gravity for the entire Data Center segment. Koopmans carried that institutional memory into the combined company.

## The CFO Transition at the Inflection Point

If the Koopmans appointment reflected the integration-era logic of the Murphy transformation programme, the CFO transition of September 2024 reflected a different kind of strategic calibration. Willem Meintjes joined Marvell as Chief Financial Officer in that month, succeeding Jean Hu, at a moment when the company's financial narrative was shifting materially. The Data Center segment was posting quarterly growth rates that placed custom AI silicon at the centre of investor attention, and the forward revenue guidance being issued from Murphy's quarterly earnings calls was increasingly dominated by the ramp timelines and programme cadences of a small number of hyperscaler custom-silicon relationships.

Meintjes arrived from Pure Storage, where he had served as CFO, and brought with him both the experience of scaling an enterprise technology company through public-market cycles and, from his earlier career at Cisco, a deeper familiarity with the networking-industry dynamics that inform how hyperscaler customers think about silicon procurement and multi-year infrastructure investment. The CFO transition, which was announced in the summer of 2024 and effective in September, came at the moment when Marvell's financial planning was becoming dominated by the economics of multi-year custom-silicon co-development programmes — an environment in which the CFO's ability to model long-duration, high-concentration, co-investment revenue streams with single-customer risk factors was materially different from the segment-diversified chip company that had preceded it.

## The Segment General Managers: Acquisition Pedigrees at Work

The three Executive Vice Presidents who lead Marvell's principal Data Center product lines each carry acquisition pedigrees that track directly to the M&A programme Murphy assembled.

Sandeep Bharathi, Executive Vice President for Custom Compute and Storage, leads the organisation through which the company's custom-ASIC relationships with Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are managed. The custom-silicon programmes — including Amazon's Trainium artificial-intelligence training accelerator and Microsoft's Maia programme — flow through Bharathi's organisation along with the advanced-process-node and packaging expertise that makes those programmes executable at scale. Marvell's work at three-nanometre and emerging two-nanometre nodes at TSMC, combined with Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate packaging variants suited to large AI accelerator die, represents a significant capital commitment and technical capability depth that sits within Bharathi's purview. The economics of the custom-silicon model — lower initial margins than merchant silicon, but deep customer stickiness and multi-generation design wins — make the custom-compute EVP one of the most strategically consequential roles in the company.

Loi Nguyen leads the Electro-Optics business as Executive Vice President, drawing on the intellectual property and customer relationships that entered Marvell through the April 2021 Inphi acquisition — a transaction that closed at approximately $10 billion and represented the largest single capital commitment of the Murphy era. Inphi had built a dominant position in pulse-amplitude modulation digital signal processors for optical interconnects used inside hyperscaler data centres — the technology that translates electrical signals into the optical pulses that move data across the intra-data-centre fabric at 100, 400, 800, and now 1,600 gigabits per second.
