But Marvell had demonstrated, across the Trainium and Maia engagements, that it could manage programme complexity at the tier-one hyperscaler level — a credential that created defensible differentiation in the sales cycle for the next generation of engagements, where programme history weighed heavily in vendor selection.

## 1.6T optics: from qualification to volume inflection

The electro-optics franchise inherited through the $10 billion Inphi acquisition had already navigated two generational transitions — from 100G to 400G, and from 400G to 800G — before the 1.6T wave arrived. Each transition had concentrated the DSP market around fewer suppliers capable of delivering the performance envelope, power budget, and manufacturing yield that hyperscalers demanded at volume. Marvell's position had strengthened, rather than eroded, at each prior node.

The 1.6T transition carried structurally larger economics. As data centre interconnect speeds doubled again, average selling prices per DSP unit increased, integration complexity favoured established suppliers with proven PAM-4 architectures, and qualification cycles — typically eighteen to twenty-four months at major hyperscalers — created a meaningful barrier to entry for challengers. Marvell's Orion DSP platform, developed for the 1.6T generation, had entered qualification at multiple hyperscaler customers by mid-FY2026. The transition from qualification to volume production represented the principal optical revenue catalyst for FY2027.

The demand backdrop supported the timing. Hyperscaler capital expenditure on data centre interconnect had accelerated sharply as AI training cluster sizes expanded — the transition from thousands to tens of thousands of accelerators per training cluster implied non-linear scaling of interconnect bandwidth requirements. At those cluster scales, optical interconnect was no longer an incremental upgrade; it was a structural necessity, and the DSP at the heart of each optical module was the most technically differentiated component in the bill of materials. Primary optical market research projected the 1.6T transceiver market reaching multiple billions of dollars in annual revenue by 2027-2028. Marvell's share of the DSP content within that market — anchored by the Inphi customer relationships and the Orion platform — placed it in a structurally advantaged position to capture disproportionate value.

## Switch silicon and the non-Data Center recovery

The October 2022 Innovium acquisition, at approximately $1.1 billion, brought the Teralynx switch silicon platform into Marvell's portfolio as a direct challenger to Broadcom's Tomahawk in data centre switching. The integration had been slower to surface in reported financials than the optical or custom silicon businesses, partly because the switching market cycle had itself been compressed through FY2024. By FY2026, the adoption of Ethernet fabric as the preferred interconnect for AI training clusters — driven by hyperscaler preference for open-standard alternatives to proprietary InfiniBand — had begun to create a more favourable demand environment for Teralynx. Marvell's ability to bundle switching silicon with custom AI accelerators and optical DSPs in integrated hyperscaler proposals represented a cross-sell dynamic unavailable to pure-play switching vendors.

Against the Data Center acceleration, carrier infrastructure, enterprise networking, and consumer had endured a prolonged compression through FY2024-FY2025. The FY2027-FY2028 window represented the credible recovery corridor, driven by depleted carrier inventories, the resumption of 5G infrastructure investment cycles, and normalising enterprise refresh cadences. The contribution to absolute revenue growth would not match Data Center magnitude, but recovery in these segments carried lower programme execution risk and more predictable cash generation characteristics — a relevant stabiliser in a mix otherwise dominated by custom programme ramp volatility.

## Risks to the FY2030 horizon

The four-year outlook carried identifiable risks that warranted parallel weight alongside the base case. Programme concentration was the most structurally significant: two or three hyperscaler engagements represented the dominant share of the custom AI silicon revenue trajectory. A reprioritisation of Amazon's Trainium roadmap or Microsoft's Maia investment — driven by AI strategy shifts, capex reallocation, or technical setbacks — would create a revenue gap difficult to replace within the window of a single fiscal year. Marvell was actively broadening its programme base to address this concentration, but the qualification-to-ramp timeline for a new hyperscaler engagement typically ran two to three years.

The second structural risk was technological disruption to the optical DSP model itself. Co-packaged optics — embedding optical components directly within the switch ASIC package rather than in discrete transceivers — threatened to alter the supply chain in ways that might disadvantage standalone DSP suppliers over the FY2028-FY2030 timeframe. Marvell had been developing co-packaged optics capability, but the technology's commercial timeline remained uncertain and the competitive dynamics of that transition were unresolved as of the snapshot date.

Execution risk on programme delivery — schedule slippage, yield issues, or performance shortfalls on major custom silicon or optical programmes — remained a permanent feature of the model. And the demonstrated sensitivity of hyperscaler capital expenditure to broader macroeconomic conditions, visible during the 2022-2023 digestion cycle, served as a reminder that AI infrastructure investment was not structurally immune to external pressures.

## The durability question

Entering the FY2027-FY2030 corridor, Marvell's central claim was that it had assembled — through a decade of disciplined acquisition and organic investment under Murphy's tenure — the only integrated custom silicon and hyperscaler optics franchise positioned outside the Nvidia-Broadcom duopoly. The Inphi-derived DSP IP, the Avera-origin custom ASIC methodology, and the accumulated hyperscaler programme credibility were assets whose replication required years of investment and customer relationship depth that no new entrant could compress.

The honest qualification was that the franchise's durability would be measured not by its current programme wins but by whether Marvell could secure the third and fourth generations of hyperscaler engagements — the custom silicon programmes for AI training and inference architectures whose specifications did not yet exist on any public roadmap. In that competition, incumbency helped but did not guarantee continuity. Murphy had spent a decade building a company capable of making that argument with tangible evidence. The next four years would determine whether the evidence accumulated faster than the risks materialised.

## Appendix C — Custom AI Silicon Programmes

Marvell's three disclosed hyperscaler custom-silicon relationships at the snapshot date were as follows.

**Amazon Trainium.** Marvell co-developed the Trainium training accelerator for Amazon Web Services. The engagement anchors the Marvell custom-compute franchise and represents one of the earliest and most strategically consequential hyperscaler ASIC partnerships in the company's history.

**Microsoft Maia.** Marvell co-developed the Maia training and inference accelerator for Microsoft Azure. The Maia programme sits alongside the Trainium engagement as the principal forward revenue driver within the Data Center segment.

**Google TPU-adjacent programmes.** Marvell has disclosed participation in custom silicon development with Google, with specific programme details not fully enumerated in public filings at the snapshot date.

Additional emerging hyperscaler programmes are referenced in investor-day materials but not individually named in Marvell public disclosures as of the frozen window.

leadership.key_finding: Marvell's executive bench reflects the deliberate eight-year transformation from a Sutardja-era networking-and-storage chip vendor into a hyperscaler custom-silicon partner under Matt Murphy. Murphy joined as CEO in July 2016 from Maxim Integrated where he had been a Group President; the M&A programme of his tenure (Cavium 2018, Avera 2019, Inphi 2020, Innovium 2022) brought in the technology and customer relationships that now anchor the Data Center segment. The current executive team layers Murphy's strategic continuity with a President and COO function under Chris Koopmans (a Cavium acquisition import), a CFO function under Willem Meintjes (joined September 2024 from Pure Storage), and deep technology leadership across the inherited acquisition pedigrees. leadership.board_composition_observation: Marvell's board pairs Chairman van Zadelhoff (security-and-enterprise-IT CEO experience) and CEO Murphy with directors who bring relevant operational and industry depth: Brown for Arm architecture, Buss for technology-industry CFO governance, Mayer for AI-and-cloud cross-board pattern recognition (her OpenAI board seat being the most consequential single connection), Frank for semiconductor-systems engineering, Switz for communications infrastructure, Morris for HR governance at scale, and Tamer for Inphi-product-line continuity.
